Monsoon Floods Disrupt Myanmar’s Economy, Supply Chains Face Major Strain

Heavy monsoon rains have triggered severe flooding across central and southern Myanmar, disrupting key transport links, submerging farmland, and forcing thousands of residents to evacuate. The disaster, which began late last week and is still unfolding, has already inundated parts of the Ayeyarwady, Bago, and Yangon regions, with river levels surpassing critical thresholds in several districts.

According to the Ministry of Social Welfare, over 100,000 people have been displaced so far, with at least seven provinces declaring states of emergency. Rail and road closures have stalled the movement of goods between Yangon and Mandalay, Myanmar’s two largest commercial centers. “What we are witnessing is an unprecedented interruption to domestic supply chains,” said U Thura Min, spokesperson for the Myanmar Chamber of Commerce. “Transport routes for essential goods and exports are largely underwater.”

Rice and pulse exports, traditionally a mainstay of Myanmar’s economy, are likely to see significant shipment delays. Textile manufacturers in the Hlaingthaya industrial zone reported suspending operations due to power outages and flooded warehouses. “We’ve halted production for at least three days and are assessing damages,” said Daw Hnin Ei, operations manager at Eastern Star Textiles.

Economic analysts warn the floods could shave up to 0.4% off Myanmar’s GDP growth this quarter, depending on the duration and severity of the crisis. The Myanmar Federation of Trade Unions has called for urgent government intervention to assist affected workers and restore critical infrastructure. With more rain forecast in the coming days, authorities are bracing for the humanitarian and economic toll to rise further.
